source: About 20% of genes are positively selected with the more conservative M1a vs. M2a tests or M2a vs M2a_fixed tests, with large overlaps among the genes identified.
evidence: The statement is based on the results presented in the text.

claim: The less conservative M7 vs. M8 tests show much greater proportions of positively selected genes (~70%).

claim: HyPhy's BUSTED identified ~ 50% of genes as positively selected.

claim: 14% of analyzed genes are found to be under positive selection in all tests.

evidence: The statement is based on the results presented in Table 2 and supplementary files.

claim: The high-confidence positive selection gene set has overall higher distributions of M0 model ω values compared to all other genes.
source: Compared to all other genes, the high-confidence positive selection gene set has overall higher distributions of M0 model ω values, which assumes a single ω for all sites in a gene (Figure 2A; Mann-Whitney U-test: gene trees: not-significant median ω = 0.084, significant median ω = 0.344, p<0.0001; species trees: not-significant ω = 0.084, significant ω = 0.332, p<0.0001).
evidence: The statement is based on the results shown in Figure 2A and statistical tests.

claim: Gene trees and species trees had similar distributions of overall ω values with the M0 model.
source: Gene trees and species trees also had similar distributions of overall ω values with the M0 model (K-S test: D = 0.006, p=1, Figure 2B).
evidence: The statement is based on the results shown in Figure 2B and statistical tests.

claim: The mean ω value is 0.15 using either the gene or species tree as the input tree.
source: The mean ω value is 0.15, the median ω is 0.10 and standard deviation is 0.14 using either the gene or species tree as the input tree.
evidence: The statement is based on the results presented in the text.

claim: The median ω value is 0.10 using either the gene or species tree as the input tree.
source: The mean ω value is 0.15, the median ω is 0.10 and standard deviation is 0.14 using either the gene or species tree as the input tree.
evidence: The statement is based on the results presented in the text.

claim: Alignment length has a significant effect on the ability to detect selection in a gene.
source: The model was significant for both gene trees (median length under selection = 1,818; median length not under selection = 1,089; coefficient = 3.49e-4, p-value<0.0001) and species trees (median length under selection = 1,893; median length not under selection = 1,158; coefficient = 3.46e-4, p-value<0.0001), likely indicating that power to detect selection increases with alignment length.
evidence: The statement is based on logistic regression results and Figure 2C.

claim: 351 genes of the high-confidence positive selection gene set could be mapped to KEGG pathways using chicken as the reference organism.

claim: PC1 from the PCA of aBS-REL parameter estimates is significantly correlated with log-transformed body mass.

claim: There is a significant overlap in positively-selected genes between birds and mammals at all four different FDR-corrected p-value cutoffs.

claim: The overlap in positively selected genes between birds and mammals is stronger at smaller FDR-corrected p-values.

claim: The overlap in positively selected genes between birds and mammals cannot be explained by constraint bias or alignment length.

claim: Pathways with immune function, particularly viral-interacting pathways, are significantly enriched for shared signatures of selection between birds and mammals.

claim: For all pathogens tested, up-regulated genes in birds are significantly more likely to be positively selected.

source: Although there are some differences in the fine details between avian and mammalian immune systems (e.g. different TLRs are functionally similar in the types of pathogens they recognize (Kaiser, 2010; Chen et al., 2013), the overall immune responses are conserved between the clades (Kaiser, 2010).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Kaiser, 2010.

claim: Pathogens are constrained in how they can interact with immune networks to suppress an immune response.

evidence: The statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Geoghegan et al., 2017; Shi et al., 2018; Henzy et al., 2014.

claim: A recent study observed higher rates of adaptation in viral genes only across populations of Drosophila melanogaster, not immune genes in general, bacterial genes, or fungal genes.

claim: Pathogens are one of the strongest selective pressures on amino acid sequence of protein coding genes in birds.

evidence: The statement is an inference based on the results presented.

claim: Site test results suggest that host-pathogen interactions are constrained to target specific sites in the same genes in different species.
source: Our site test results, which require the same sites to be under selection across species, suggest that host-pathogen interactions are constrained to target specific sites in the same genes in different species.
evidence: The statement is an inference based on the site test results.

claim: Five of the 10 avian TLRs are present in the dataset.
source: Five of the 10 avian TLRs are present in our dataset, with TLRs 1A, 1B, 2A, and 2B likely filtered out due to their recent duplication and TLR21 likely filtered out due to missing data caused by sequencing difficulty (Alcaide and Edwards, 2011; Grueber et al., 2014).

claim: TLR5 has the highest proportion of selected sites among avian TLRs.
source: In addition, our results confirm those of Alcaide and Edwards, 2011; Grueber et al., 2014, and Velová et al. (2018), which showed TLR5 as having the highest proportion of selected sites, and the endosomal TLRs (TLR3, TLR7) as having the smallest proportion of selected sites.

claim: The endosomal TLRs (TLR3, TLR7) have the smallest proportion of selected sites among avian TLRs.

evidence: The statement is based on the results and citations to previous studies.

claim: TRIF (TICAM1) is the gene with the highest proportion of significant lineages in birds in the Influenza A pathway.

evidence: The statement is based on the aBS-REL results.

claim: TRIF is under selection in 61% of avian lineages.
source: This gene is under selection in 61% of avian lineages, one of the highest proportions in our dataset, and highlights that genes beyond the classically studied MHC loci and TLRs may be interesting candidates for future studies on the ecology and evolution of host-pathogen co-evolution.

claim: Birds are known for their compact genomes that show greater than average chromosomal stability.

evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2014b; Cui et al., 2014; Kapusta and Suh, 2017.

claim: Birds show a surprising paucity of transposable elements.

evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Cui et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014b; Kapusta and Suh, 2017.

evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Cui et al., 2014.

evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to Kapusta et al., 2017.

claim: Steroid hormone biosynthesis is known to be related to diverse life history strategies in birds.

claim: Linoleic acid is related to thermoregulation and can vary across habitats in birds.

evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Ben-Hamo et al., 2013; Andersson et al., 2015.

claim: The genetics of the avian visual system has traditionally focused on the evolution of the cone receptor genes.
